## 4. Derivation Chains

### C1 — What job would a free tier actually do here?

```text
GT-2 (outbound+referral only, no inbound channel) + GT-6 (revenue impact ≈ N × r × LTV)
→ a free tier's revenue contribution requires nonzero top-of-funnel signup volume N
→ that signup volume is currently ≈0 per GT-2, because no mechanism routes visitors to a signup page at any volume
→ therefore a free tier cannot presently function as a distribution/acquisition mechanism for this company — it has nothing to convert
→ its only remaining candidate jobs are competitive-parity signaling (addressed in C3) or a PLG motion that would first require building the missing inbound engine (A-2), which is a separate, larger project than "add a free tier"
```
**Pre-check:** head = GT-2 (unsuffixed) · GT-6 (unsuffixed) · ?-marked = none · lowest cited = none · Inputs ceiling = HIGH
**Confidence: HIGH.** Inputs are both unsuffixed ground truths; inference is a direct application of a definitional identity (GT-6) to a stipulated fact (GT-2); no live rival reading of this specific chain — the only way N is nonzero today is referral traffic landing on a public signup page, which GT-2 says does not exist as a channel.

### C2 — Cost/NPV model: what has to be true for a free tier to be NPV-positive

```text
GT-3 (cost scales with active users, not payers) + GT-7? (cost/active-free-user, $50–500/yr, mid $200) + GT-8? (avg. 1.5 yr tenure as free before converting/churning) + GT-9? (LTV of a converted customer, $9K–24K, mid $15K)
→ a free tier carries a guaranteed, non-zero cost for every active free user regardless of conversion
→ breakeven free-to-paid conversion rate r* solves N·r·LTV = N·c·t, and N cancels out of the equation entirely
→ r* = (c × t) / LTV — breakeven conversion rate depends only on cost-per-user, tenure, and converted LTV, not on funnel volume
→ at central estimates, r* = ($200 × 1.5) / $15,000 ≈ 2.0%; at the pessimistic-cost end, r* = ($500 × 1.5) / $9,000 ≈ 8.3%; at the optimistic-cost end, r* = ($50 × 1.5) / $24,000 ≈ 0.3%
→ 2% sits inside the range typically cited for B2B self-serve freemium conversion (roughly 1–5%), so the unit economics are plausible but not safely so — the breakeven rate is highly sensitive to the GT-7?/GT-8?/GT-9? estimate brackets, none of which this company has measured directly [Assumes: A-10]
```
**Pre-check:** head = GT-3 (unsuffixed) · GT-7? · GT-8? · GT-9? (all `?`) · ?-marked = GT-7, GT-8, GT-9 · lowest cited = none (no chains cited) · Inputs ceiling = MEDIUM
**Confidence: MEDIUM.** Would be HIGH if the Inputs axis weren't carrying three `?`-marked estimate inputs; the arithmetic identity (Inference axis) is sound and not in dispute. What would remove the cap: replacing GT-7?/GT-8?/GT-9? with this company's own measured figures from a pilot (chain C5) — that is precisely the "no pilot data" gap named in GT-4, and it is the single biggest lever on this chain's confidence. **Key structural insight (independent of the exact bracket): breakeven viability does not depend on funnel volume N — it depends only on cost-per-user, tenure, and converted LTV.** This matters for C1: even if C1's funnel problem were solved tomorrow, C2's unit economics would still need to clear ~2–8% conversion before volume helps rather than hurts.

### C3 — Is "competitors all have a free tier" real evidence of necessity?

```text
GT-5 (all named competitors have a free tier)
→ the competitor set was selected because they compete in this category — a free tier may be structural to their own (possibly lower-ACV, higher-volume, self-serve) GTM motion rather than evidence that any GTM motion needs one
→ no win/loss data is cited showing a lost deal where the prospect named "no free tier" as the reason
→ therefore GT-5 is weak evidence for this company's specific question and is better read as a mimicry/survivorship signal than a demand signal
```
**Pre-check:** head = GT-5 (unsuffixed) · ?-marked on head = none · dependency note: Inference rests on [Assumes: A-3?], an unverified assumption not itself a head identifier · lowest cited = none · Inputs ceiling = HIGH on Inputs alone, held to MEDIUM by the Inference axis per A-3?
**Confidence: MEDIUM.** The logical critique of the parity argument is sound (Inference axis is clean), but the chain cannot rule out that *some* lost deals genuinely did hinge on "try before you buy" friction — that would require win/loss interview data this company does not currently collect on this question. What would raise this to HIGH: running a lightweight win/loss review on the next 10–20 closed-lost outbound deals, explicitly asking whether a free/trial option would have changed the outcome.

### C4 — Second-order sales-motion risk (actor lens + time lens)

```text
GT-2 (consultative outbound motion, no existing self-serve exit ramp)
→ [Assumes: A-5] introducing any free/self-serve option gives an active-pipeline prospect a lower-commitment alternative to a signed $10K/yr contract
→ actor lens: sales reps may lean on "just try the free tier" to avoid a hard close conversation, shifting their own behavior away from the quota-driving motion that built GT-1's $2.4M ARR; procurement-side buyers may stall a decision pending self-service evaluation, lengthening cycle time
→ time lens: in the first 1–2 quarters this shows up as minor friction; if unmanaged for a year or more it can quietly re-shape the GTM motion into a hybrid the sales org was never comped or structured for (an org-design second-order effect, not just a revenue one) [Assumes: A-11]
→ this risk is real but containable — it is a reason to bound any experiment (trial, not perpetual access) and to keep the sales team, not a public signup page, as the gatekeeper of who gets it (see C5/C6)
```
**Pre-check:** head = GT-2 (unsuffixed) · ?-marked on head = none · dependency note: Inference rests on [Assumes: A-5?, A-11?], both unverified and not head identifiers · lowest cited = none · Inputs ceiling = HIGH on Inputs alone, held to MEDIUM by the Inference axis per A-5?/A-11?
**Confidence: MEDIUM.** The mechanism is well-established in B2B SaaS generally (Inference axis reasonably strong) but its magnitude for *this* sales team and *this* buyer profile is unverified (A-5 is untested) — what would resolve it: measuring sales-cycle length and realized ACV for trial-attached deals vs. non-trial deals during the pilot in C5/C6, which is exactly the tripwire built into the pre-mortem (process output, Adversarial pass record).

### C5 — Trade-off analysis: cheapest way to get real signal

Four options scored against six weighted criteria (full table and flip test are process output in this run; the collapsed result is reported here per the output template's §4 conversion rule). Options: **A** status quo (no pilot, no free tier); **B** time-boxed full-feature trial attached to existing outbound/referral leads; **C** full self-serve freemium launch; **D** perpetual free tier scoped to a narrow, non-core ICP segment.

```text
GT-2 (no inbound channel, no self-serve infra) + GT-3 (cost scales with active users, open-ended exposure risk)
→ option C requires building the self-serve signup/metering/billing/upgrade infrastructure GT-2 confirms does not exist, and exposes GT-3's open-ended cost with the least-informative signal (volume will be near-zero anyway absent an inbound engine, and any data that does arrive conflates "no funnel" with "bad conversion economics")
→ option B reuses the existing outbound/referral funnel, bounds GT-3's cost exposure to a fixed trial window, and isolates the one unknown that actually matters here (GT-4's missing conversion rate) without also having to solve the funnel problem at the same time
→ weighted trade-off scoring (Signal quality, Build cost, Cost exposure, Sales-risk, Speed, Reversibility; weights 5/4/4/4/3/3) ranks B highest (102) ahead of A (83), D (61), C (34) [Assumes: A-12]
→ flip test: zeroing the single highest-leverage criterion for B (Signal quality, weight 5) still leaves B ahead of A by 4 points — no single-criterion weight change in the plausible range reverses the ranking; B is a robust choice, not a near-tie
→ therefore the cheapest path to real signal is a time-boxed trial attached to the existing sales motion, not a narrow-ICP pilot and not a full freemium launch
```
**Pre-check:** head = GT-2 (unsuffixed) · GT-3 (unsuffixed) · ?-marked = none on this chain's direct head (the trade-off's own inputs reuse GT-2/GT-3 directly; A-5/A-8 inform scoring rationale but are not head identifiers) · lowest cited = none · Inputs ceiling = HIGH
**Confidence: HIGH.** Inputs are unsuffixed ground truths; the trade-off procedure's weights were locked before scoring (per the procedure's discipline) and the flip test shows the ranking survives the largest plausible single-criterion perturbation. Rival considered and ruled out: "skip straight to full freemium because competitors already validated the model" — ruled out by C3 (competitor parity is weak evidence of transferability) and by C1 (the funnel precondition is absent regardless of what competitors validated elsewhere) — see §5 Abandoned Reasoning.

### C6 — Conditional recommendation with go/no-go thresholds

```text
C2 (breakeven r* ≈ 0.3–8.3%, central ≈2%, MEDIUM) + C5 (time-boxed trial is the robust choice, HIGH)
→ run a time-boxed (e.g., 30-day) full-feature trial attached to sales-qualified outbound/referral leads, not an open public signup
→ pre-commit, before launch, to explicit go/no-go thresholds derived from C2: proceed toward a broader/permanent free tier only if measured conversion r ≥ r* for the measured cost-per-active-trial-user, sustained across at least two cohorts
→ pre-mortem findings (process output, Adversarial pass record) attach four tripwires with named owners to this plan: decision-date discipline (Finance/exec), sales-cycle-length delta (Sales lead), cost-per-user overrun (Support/Ops lead), extension-request rate (Product/CS)
→ this converts GT-4's "no pilot data" gap into a bounded, owned, time-limited experiment rather than either an indefinite "no" or an uninstrumented "yes"
```
**Pre-check:** head = C2 (MEDIUM) · C5 (HIGH) · ?-marked = none directly on this chain's head (the `?` inputs are inherited through C2, already priced into C2's own band) · lowest cited = MEDIUM (C2) · Inputs ceiling = MEDIUM
**Confidence: MEDIUM**, capped by C2's MEDIUM (a chain is capped at the lowest-rated chain its head cites). What would remove the cap: the pilot itself (this chain's own recommendation) producing measured, company-specific values for GT-7?/GT-8?/GT-9?, at which point C2 — and therefore C6 — can be re-rated HIGH or re-rated down to a clear LOW/no-go, either of which is a strictly better state than today's unresolved MEDIUM.

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

**What was tried:** Treat "skip the pilot and go straight to a full self-serve freemium launch, since every named competitor already validated the model" as the leading option.
**Why abandoned:** This conflates two distinct claims — "freemium works for category X" and "freemium works for *this company's* GTM motion." C1 shows the structural precondition (an inbound funnel to convert) is absent regardless of what competitors proved elsewhere; C3 shows the competitor-parity signal itself is weak (mimicry/survivorship, no win/loss evidence); C5's trade-off scoring ranks this option lowest of the four on signal quality, cost exposure, and reversibility (score 34 vs. 102 for the trial option).
**What it ruled out:** Full freemium launch (option C) as the near-term move; it remains a theoretically available later step only after the inbound-funnel precondition is separately solved and the pilot (C6) clears its thresholds.

**What was tried:** Treat the narrow-ICP perpetual free tier (option D — e.g., free for a non-core segment such as single-seat or hobbyist users) as a way to get real freemium signal without touching the core sales motion.
**Why abandoned:** It still requires building meaningful self-serve infrastructure (A-8 — this is not "just a pricing page"), carries GT-3's open-ended cost exposure (no time box), and the resulting conversion signal would come from a segment that is not the $10K-ACV buyer GT-1 is anchored to — so it answers a narrower, less decision-relevant question than C5's chosen option. Trade-off scoring (C5) ranked it third of four (61 vs. 102).
**What it ruled out:** A narrow-ICP permanent free tier as the *first* move; it remains a plausible *second* experiment if the core-motion trial (C6) succeeds and a genuinely distinct underserved segment is later identified.

**What was tried:** Treat "do nothing, indefinitely" (option A, status quo) as an acceptable permanent answer rather than a temporary default.
**Why abandoned:** Status quo scores well on every axis except the two that matter for resolving GT-4's actual gap — Signal quality and Speed to data (score 1 of 5 on each) — meaning it preserves optionality but never retires the uncertainty the user explicitly asked this analysis to address. C5's trade-off result (B beats A by 19 points, robust under the flip test) shows a bounded trial strictly dominates indefinite inaction once cost-exposure is controlled for.
**What it ruled out:** Permanent inaction as the final answer; it remains correct only as the fallback if C2's pessimistic-cost bracket is confirmed (see Section 6's flip condition for an outright "no").

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Do not launch a permanent or full self-serve free tier now. Instead, run a time-boxed (≈30-day) full-feature trial attached to sales-qualified outbound and referral leads — reusing the existing funnel rather than building a new one — with pre-committed go/no-go conversion and cost thresholds and four named, owned tripwires (decision-date discipline, sales-cycle-length delta, cost-per-user overrun, extension-request rate) (chain C6). Use the pilot's measured results to replace this analysis's estimated cost-model inputs (chain C2) with real numbers before deciding on anything broader.

**Key insight:** A free tier is a *conversion* mechanism, not a *demand-generation* mechanism — its revenue impact is the product of funnel volume, conversion rate, and converted LTV, and if funnel volume is zero the other two terms are irrelevant (chain C1). This company's GTM motion (outbound + referral, GT-2) currently supplies that volume at or near zero for a public free tier, which is why "add a free tier" is the wrong frame; "get a company-specific conversion-rate measurement cheaply, inside the motion that already works" (chain C5/C6) is the right one.

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** The recommended trial is not free of risk — it carries real, if bounded, sales-cycle-lengthening and cost-overrun exposure (chain C4), and it deliberately defers the two biggest upside scenarios (a real inbound/PLG motion, or full competitive parity) rather than capturing them immediately. It also does not resolve the "competitors all have one" perception question (chain C3) — a prospect who wants to self-serve evaluate today still cannot, during the trial design and rollout window.

**Pre-check:** head = C1 (HIGH) · C2 (MEDIUM) · C3 (MEDIUM) · C4 (MEDIUM) · C5 (HIGH) · C6 (MEDIUM) · GT-N? rested on directly = none beyond those already inside the cited chains · ?-marked = none new · lowest cited = MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling = MEDIUM
**Confidence: MEDIUM.** The structural argument against a full freemium launch today (C1, C5) is HIGH-confidence and not sensitive to the unresolved estimates. The conditional "run a trial, with these thresholds" recommendation is capped at MEDIUM by C2's unresolved cost/conversion brackets (GT-7?/GT-8?/GT-9?) and by C4's unverified cannibalization magnitude (A-5?) — both are exactly what the recommended trial (C6) is designed to resolve. Rivals: the strongest live rival — "skip the pilot, go straight to full freemium because competitors already proved it" — is ruled out in §5. No rival currently threatens the narrower claim that *some* instrumented, bounded experiment beats both permanent inaction and an uninstrumented full launch.

**Flip conditions:**
- **Flips to YES (broader/permanent free tier):** the pilot (C6) measures a sustained free-to-paid conversion rate at or above the breakeven r* implied by the *measured* (not estimated) cost-per-active-user and converted LTV, across at least two cohorts, **and** no material sales-cycle lengthening or realized-ACV erosion is observed (C4's risk does not materialize), **and** a genuine inbound-traffic source (content, SEO, community, partner-driven, or organic referral growth) exists or is concurrently built — because C1's volume term must be nonzero for any of this to matter at scale.
- **Flips to an outright NO, without even running the pilot:** Finance produces a measured (not estimated) cost-per-active-free-user high enough that the resulting breakeven r* exceeds realistic B2B self-serve conversion benchmarks (roughly >8–10%) even under optimistic LTV assumptions — in that case C2's economics fail regardless of execution quality, and the trial should not be run at all.
- **Default if neither flip condition is yet evaluated:** proceed with the bounded, instrumented trial in C6 — it is strictly better than guessing in either direction, and it is the cheapest available way to retire GT-4's "no pilot data" gap.

## 4. Derivation Chains

### C1 — What job would a free tier actually do here?

```text
GT-2? (outbound+referral only, no inbound channel) + GT-6 (revenue impact ≈ N × r × LTV)
→ a free tier's revenue contribution requires nonzero top-of-funnel signup volume N
→ that signup volume is currently ≈0 per GT-2?, because no mechanism routes visitors to a signup page at any volume
→ therefore a free tier cannot presently function as a distribution/acquisition mechanism for this company — it has nothing to convert
→ its only remaining candidate jobs are competitive-parity signaling (addressed in C3) or a PLG motion that would first require building the missing inbound engine (A-2), which is a separate, larger project than "add a free tier"
```
**Pre-check:** head = GT-2? · GT-6 (unsuffixed) · ?-marked = GT-2 · lowest cited = none · Inputs ceiling = MEDIUM
**Confidence: MEDIUM.** GT-2? is unverified under the Input Contract's provenance rule (operator-stated, no CRM/pipeline export opened by this analysis) — verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade: pull the actual marketing/sales funnel report and confirm zero self-serve signup volume exists today. The Inference axis is clean (GT-6 is a definitional identity applied directly to GT-2?) and no live rival contests this chain's endpoint — the only way N could be nonzero today is referral traffic landing on an informal signup path, and GT-2? itself (even unverified) already asserts that path does not exist.

### C2 — Cost/NPV model: what has to be true for a free tier to be NPV-positive

```text
GT-3? (cost scales with active users, not payers) + GT-7? (cost/active-free-user, $50–500/yr, mid $200) + GT-8? (avg. 1.5 yr tenure as free before converting/churning) + GT-9? (LTV of a converted customer, $9K–24K, mid $15K)
→ a free tier carries a guaranteed, non-zero cost for every active free user regardless of conversion
→ breakeven free-to-paid conversion rate r* solves N·r·LTV = N·c·t, and N cancels out of the equation entirely
→ r* = (c × t) / LTV — breakeven conversion rate depends only on cost-per-user, tenure, and converted LTV, not on funnel volume
→ at central estimates, r* = ($200 × 1.5) / $15,000 ≈ 2.0%; at the pessimistic-cost end, r* = ($500 × 1.5) / $9,000 ≈ 8.3%; at the optimistic-cost end, r* = ($50 × 1.5) / $24,000 ≈ 0.3%
→ 2% sits inside the range typically cited for B2B self-serve freemium conversion (roughly 1–5%), so the unit economics are plausible but not safely so — the breakeven rate is highly sensitive to the GT-7?/GT-8?/GT-9? estimate brackets, none of which this company has measured directly [Assumes: A-10]
```
**Pre-check:** head = GT-3? · GT-7? · GT-8? · GT-9? (all `?`) · ?-marked = GT-3, GT-7, GT-8, GT-9 · lowest cited = none (no chains cited) · Inputs ceiling = MEDIUM
**Confidence: MEDIUM.** Four `?`-marked inputs, each with its own removal path: GT-3? — verification: obtain Finance's own documented cost-allocation report rather than the operator's summary of it; GT-7?/GT-8?/GT-9? — verification: replace each estimate bracket with this company's own measured figures from the recommended pilot (chain C5/C6), which is precisely the "no pilot data" gap GT-4? names. The arithmetic identity itself (Inference axis) is sound and recomputes cleanly (see Adversarial pass, process output). **Key structural insight (independent of the exact bracket): breakeven viability does not depend on funnel volume N — it depends only on cost-per-user, tenure, and converted LTV.** This matters for C1: even if C1's funnel problem were solved tomorrow, C2's unit economics would still need to clear roughly 2–8% conversion before volume helps rather than hurts.

### C3 — Is "competitors all have a free tier" real evidence of necessity?

```text
GT-5? (all named competitors have a free tier)
→ the competitor set was selected because they compete in this category — a free tier may be structural to their own (possibly lower-ACV, higher-volume, self-serve) GTM motion rather than evidence that any GTM motion needs one
→ no win/loss data is cited showing a lost deal where the prospect named "no free tier" as the reason
→ therefore GT-5? is weak evidence for this company's specific question and is better read as a mimicry/survivorship signal than a demand signal
```
**Pre-check:** head = GT-5? · ?-marked = GT-5 · lowest cited = none · Inputs ceiling = MEDIUM
**Confidence: MEDIUM.** GT-5? is unverified — this analysis did not independently check competitor pricing pages; verification: have someone confirm each named competitor's current public pricing page still shows a free tier, since competitive offerings change. Independently, the chain's own rival is live and unresolved: [Assumes: A-3] some closed-lost deals may genuinely have hinged on "try before you buy" friction, and no win-loss interview data exists to settle it — verification: run a lightweight win-loss review on the next 10–20 closed-lost outbound deals, explicitly asking whether a free/trial option would have changed the outcome.

### C4 — Second-order sales-motion risk (actor lens + time lens)

```text
GT-2? (consultative outbound motion, no existing self-serve exit ramp)
→ [Assumes: A-5] introducing any free/self-serve option gives an active-pipeline prospect a lower-commitment alternative to a signed $10K/yr contract
→ actor lens: sales reps may lean on "just try the free tier" to avoid a hard close conversation, shifting their own behavior away from the quota-driving motion that built GT-1?'s $2.4M ARR; procurement-side buyers may stall a decision pending self-service evaluation, lengthening cycle time
→ time lens: in the first 1–2 quarters this shows up as minor friction; if unmanaged for a year or more it can quietly re-shape the GTM motion into a hybrid the sales org was never comped or structured for (an org-design second-order effect, not just a revenue one) [Assumes: A-11]
→ this risk is real but containable — it is a reason to bound any experiment (trial, not perpetual access) and to keep the sales team, not a public signup page, as the gatekeeper of who gets it (see C5/C6)
```
**Pre-check:** head = GT-2? · ?-marked = GT-2 · lowest cited = none · Inputs ceiling = MEDIUM
**Confidence: MEDIUM.** GT-2? is unverified (same cause and verification path as C1). Independently, [Assumes: A-5] and [Assumes: A-11] are both untested — the cannibalization mechanism is well-established in B2B SaaS generally, but its magnitude for *this* sales team and buyer profile is unmeasured; verification: track sales-cycle length and realized ACV for trial-attached deals vs. non-trial deals during the pilot in C5/C6 — this is exactly the tripwire built into the pre-mortem (process output, Adversarial pass record).

### C5 — Trade-off analysis: cheapest way to get real signal

Four options scored against six weighted criteria (full table and flip test are process output in this run; the collapsed result is reported here per the output template's §4 conversion rule). Options: **A** status quo (no pilot, no free tier); **B** time-boxed full-feature trial attached to existing outbound/referral leads; **C** full self-serve freemium launch; **D** perpetual free tier scoped to a narrow, non-core ICP segment.

```text
GT-2? (no inbound channel, no self-serve infra) + GT-3? (cost scales with active users, open-ended exposure risk)
→ option C requires building the self-serve signup/metering/billing/upgrade infrastructure GT-2? describes as absent, and exposes GT-3?'s cost pattern with the least-informative signal (volume will be near-zero anyway absent an inbound engine, and any data that does arrive conflates "no funnel" with "bad conversion economics")
→ option B reuses the existing outbound/referral funnel, bounds the cost exposure GT-3? describes to a fixed trial window, and isolates the one unknown that actually matters here (GT-4?'s missing conversion rate) without also having to solve the funnel problem at the same time
→ weighted trade-off scoring (Signal quality, Build cost, Cost exposure, Sales-risk, Speed, Reversibility; weights 5/4/4/4/3/3) ranks B highest (102) ahead of A (83), D (61), C (34) [Assumes: A-12]
→ flip test: zeroing the single highest-leverage criterion for B (Signal quality, weight 5) still leaves B ahead of A by 4 points — no single-criterion weight change in the plausible range reverses the ranking; B is a robust choice, not a near-tie
→ therefore the cheapest path to real signal is a time-boxed trial attached to the existing sales motion, not a narrow-ICP pilot and not a full freemium launch
```
**Pre-check:** head = GT-2? · GT-3? · ?-marked = GT-2, GT-3 · lowest cited = none · Inputs ceiling = MEDIUM
**Confidence: MEDIUM.** GT-2? and GT-3? are both unverified under the Input Contract's provenance rule (same cause as C1/C4: operator-stated, no source opened by this analysis); verification: the funnel/pipeline export (for GT-2?) and Finance's own documented cost-allocation report (for GT-3?), as named on C1 and C2's own confidence lines. Independently of that cap, the trade-off procedure's own discipline is sound: weights were locked before scoring, and the flip test shows the ranking survives the largest plausible single-criterion perturbation, so the choice among options is robust even though the underlying GTs carry the formal `?`. Rival considered and ruled out: "skip straight to full freemium because competitors already validated the model" — ruled out by C3 (competitor parity is weak evidence of transferability) and by C1 (the funnel precondition is absent regardless of what competitors validated elsewhere) — see §5 Abandoned Reasoning.

### C6 — Conditional recommendation with go/no-go thresholds

```text
C2 (breakeven r* ≈ 0.3–8.3%, central ≈2%, MEDIUM) + C5 (time-boxed trial is the robust choice, MEDIUM)
→ run a time-boxed (e.g., 30-day) full-feature trial attached to sales-qualified outbound/referral leads, not an open public signup
→ pre-commit, before launch, to explicit go/no-go thresholds derived from C2: proceed toward a broader/permanent free tier only if measured conversion r ≥ r* for the measured cost-per-active-trial-user, sustained across at least two cohorts
→ pre-mortem findings (process output, Adversarial pass record) attach four tripwires with named owners to this plan: decision-date discipline (Finance/exec), sales-cycle-length delta (Sales lead), cost-per-user overrun (Support/Ops lead), extension-request rate (Product/CS)
→ this converts GT-4?'s "no pilot data" gap into a bounded, owned, time-limited experiment rather than either an indefinite "no" or an uninstrumented "yes"
```
**Pre-check:** head = C2 (MEDIUM) · C5 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked = none directly on this chain's head (the `?` inputs are inherited through C2 and C5, already priced into their own bands) · lowest cited = MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling = MEDIUM
**Confidence: MEDIUM**, capped at the lowest-rated chain its head cites (both C2 and C5 are MEDIUM, so there is no lower cap available and no higher one licensed either). What would remove the cap: the pilot itself (this chain's own recommendation) producing measured, company-specific, sourced values in place of GT-3?/GT-7?/GT-8?/GT-9?, at which point C2 — and therefore C6 — can be re-rated HIGH or re-rated down to a clear LOW/no-go, either of which is a strictly better state than today's unresolved MEDIUM.

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

**What was tried:** Treat "skip the pilot and go straight to a full self-serve freemium launch, since every named competitor already validated the model" as the leading option.
**Why abandoned:** This conflates two distinct claims — "freemium works for category X" and "freemium works for *this company's* GTM motion." C1 shows the structural precondition (an inbound funnel to convert) is absent regardless of what competitors proved elsewhere; C3 shows the competitor-parity signal itself is weak (mimicry/survivorship, no win/loss evidence); C5's trade-off scoring ranks this option lowest of the four on signal quality, cost exposure, and reversibility (score 34 vs. 102 for the trial option).
**What it ruled out:** Full freemium launch (option C) as the near-term move; it remains a theoretically available later step only after the inbound-funnel precondition is separately solved and the pilot (C6) clears its thresholds.

**What was tried:** Treat the narrow-ICP perpetual free tier (option D — e.g., free for a non-core segment such as single-seat or hobbyist users) as a way to get real freemium signal without touching the core sales motion.
**Why abandoned:** It still requires building meaningful self-serve infrastructure (A-8 — this is not "just a pricing page"), carries GT-3?'s open-ended cost exposure pattern (no time box), and the resulting conversion signal would come from a segment that is not the $10K-ACV buyer GT-1? is anchored to — so it answers a narrower, less decision-relevant question than C5's chosen option. Trade-off scoring (C5) ranked it third of four (61 vs. 102).
**What it ruled out:** A narrow-ICP permanent free tier as the *first* move; it remains a plausible *second* experiment if the core-motion trial (C6) succeeds and a genuinely distinct underserved segment is later identified.

**What was tried:** Treat "do nothing, indefinitely" (option A, status quo) as an acceptable permanent answer rather than a temporary default.
**Why abandoned:** Status quo scores well on every axis except the two that matter for resolving GT-4?'s actual gap — Signal quality and Speed to data (score 1 of 5 on each) — meaning it preserves optionality but never retires the uncertainty the user explicitly asked this analysis to address. C5's trade-off result (B beats A by 19 points, robust under the flip test) shows a bounded trial strictly dominates indefinite inaction once cost-exposure is controlled for.
**What it ruled out:** Permanent inaction as the final answer; it remains correct only as the fallback if C2's pessimistic-cost bracket is confirmed (see Section 6's flip condition for an outright "no").

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Do not launch a permanent or full self-serve free tier now. Instead, run a time-boxed (≈30-day) full-feature trial attached to sales-qualified outbound and referral leads — reusing the existing funnel rather than building a new one — with pre-committed go/no-go conversion and cost thresholds and four named, owned tripwires (decision-date discipline, sales-cycle-length delta, cost-per-user overrun, extension-request rate) (chain C6). Use the pilot's measured results to replace this analysis's estimated and unverified cost-model inputs (chain C2) with real, sourced numbers before deciding on anything broader.

**Key insight:** A free tier is a *conversion* mechanism, not a *demand-generation* mechanism — its revenue impact is the product of funnel volume, conversion rate, and converted LTV, and if funnel volume is zero the other two terms are irrelevant (chain C1). This company's GTM motion (outbound + referral) currently supplies that volume at or near zero for a public free tier, which is why "add a free tier" is the wrong frame; "get a company-specific conversion-rate measurement cheaply, inside the motion that already works" (chain C5/C6) is the right one.

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** The recommended trial is not free of risk — it carries real, if bounded, sales-cycle-lengthening and cost-overrun exposure (chain C4), and it deliberately defers the two biggest upside scenarios (a real inbound/PLG motion, or full competitive parity) rather than capturing them immediately. It also does not resolve the "competitors all have one" perception question (chain C3) — a prospect who wants to self-serve evaluate today still cannot, during the trial design and rollout window.

**Pre-check:** head = C1 (MEDIUM) · C2 (MEDIUM) · C3 (MEDIUM) · C4 (MEDIUM) · C5 (MEDIUM) · C6 (MEDIUM) · GT-N? rested on directly = none beyond those already inside the cited chains · ?-marked = none new · lowest cited = MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling = MEDIUM
**Confidence: MEDIUM.** Every chain this conclusion rests on (C1, C2, C3, C4, C5, C6) is rated MEDIUM, not HIGH — each one's own confidence line above names its specific cause and verification path, so this line does not re-derive them. Two distinct drivers sit behind the uniform MEDIUM: (1) a formal one — GT-1? through GT-5?, this company's own stipulated ARR/GTM/cost/competitor facts, carry `?` under the Input Contract's provenance rule because no external source (CRM export, Finance report, competitor pricing page) was opened by this analysis, even though their content is not substantively in doubt; and (2) a practical one — C2's three wide estimate brackets (GT-7?/GT-8?/GT-9?) and C4's unverified cannibalization magnitude (A-5?/A-11?), which the recommended pilot (C6) exists specifically to retire. Rivals: the strongest live rival to the headline recommendation — "skip the pilot, go straight to full freemium because competitors already proved it" — is ruled out in §5. The narrower rival still live and unresolved is C3's own: that some lost deals genuinely hinged on the lack of a trial/free option, which no win-loss data currently settles.

**Flip conditions:**
- **Flips to YES (broader/permanent free tier):** the pilot (C6) measures a sustained free-to-paid conversion rate at or above the breakeven r* implied by the *measured* (not estimated) cost-per-active-user and converted LTV, across at least two cohorts, **and** no material sales-cycle lengthening or realized-ACV erosion is observed (C4's risk does not materialize), **and** a genuine inbound-traffic source (content, SEO, community, partner-driven, or organic referral growth) exists or is concurrently built — because C1's volume term must be nonzero for any of this to matter at scale.
- **Flips to an outright NO, without even running the pilot:** Finance produces a measured (not estimated) cost-per-active-free-user high enough that the resulting breakeven r* exceeds realistic B2B self-serve conversion benchmarks (roughly >8–10%) even under optimistic LTV assumptions — in that case C2's economics fail regardless of execution quality, and the trial should not be run at all.
- **Default if neither flip condition is yet evaluated:** proceed with the bounded, instrumented trial in C6 — it is strictly better than guessing in either direction, and it is the cheapest available way to retire GT-4?'s "no pilot data" gap.
FP_EOF

A skeptic test: the triggering event was presumably "competitors all have one, should we get one too" — but the real question is not "do we need the feature" but "does this company's demand-generation and sales motion give a free tier anything to do." That is the question this analysis answers.

3	**Essence Statement:** Should this company — $2.4M ARR, 240 paying teams, ~$10,000 average ACV, acquired entirely through outbound sales and referrals, with no self-serve inbound channel — add a free tier, given that (a) free-tier infrastructure/support cost scales with *active* users regardless of whether they ever pay, and (b) no historical free-to-paid conversion data exists for this product?
4	
5	**Success criteria — a correct answer must:**
6	- Name the specific job a free tier would do for *this* company's actual go-to-market motion (distribution mechanism, competitive-parity signal, PLG motion, or something else), not a generic "freemium is good practice" claim.
7	- Produce an explicit cost/NPV model showing what conversion rate, cost-per-active-free-user, and funnel volume would need to be true for a free tier to pay for itself, anchored to the $10K ACV figure.
8	- Address the named second-order risks (sales cannibalization, support load, competitive-parity reasoning) rather than ignoring them.
9	- Identify the cheapest way to obtain real conversion signal before committing capital to a permanent free tier.
10	- Give one recommendation — which may be conditional — with explicit, falsifiable conditions that would flip it in either direction. No success criterion requires the answer to be exactly "add" or "don't add"; a conditional path is an admissible and, in this case, likely answer.
11	
12	A skeptic test: the triggering event was presumably "competitors all have one, should we get one too" — but the real question is not "do we need the feature" but "does this company's demand-generation and sales motion give a free tier anything to do." That is the question this analysis answers.

130	## 5. Abandoned Reasoning
131	
132	**What was tried:** Treat "skip the pilot and go straight to a full self-serve freemium launch, since every named competitor already validated the model" as the leading option.
133	**Why abandoned:** This conflates two distinct claims — "freemium works for category X" and "freemium works for *this company's* GTM motion." C1 shows the structural precondition (an inbound funnel to convert) is absent regardless of what competitors proved elsewhere; C3 shows the competitor-parity signal itself is weak (mimicry/survivorship, no win/loss evidence); C5's trade-off scoring ranks this option lowest of the four on signal quality, cost exposure, and reversibility (score 34 vs. 102 for the trial option).
134	**What it ruled out:** Full freemium launch (option C) as the near-term move; it remains a theoretically available later step only after the inbound-funnel precondition is separately solved and the pilot (C6) clears its thresholds.
135	
136	**What was tried:** Treat the narrow-ICP perpetual free tier (option D — e.g., free for a non-core segment such as single-seat or hobbyist users) as a way to get real freemium signal without touching the core sales motion.
137	**Why abandoned:** It still requires building meaningful self-serve infrastructure (A-8 — this is not "just a pricing page"), carries GT-3?'s open-ended cost exposure pattern (no time box), and the resulting conversion signal would come from a segment that is not the $10K-ACV buyer GT-1? is anchored to — so it answers a narrower, less decision-relevant question than C5's chosen option. 138	**What it ruled out:** A narrow-ICP permanent free tier as the *first* move; it remains a plausible *second* experiment if the core-motion trial (C6) succeeds and a genuinely distinct underserved segment is later identified.

141	**Why abandoned:** Status quo scores well on every axis except the two that matter for resolving GT-4?'s actual gap — Signal quality and Speed to data (score 1 of 5 on each) — meaning it preserves optionality but never retires the uncertainty the user explicitly asked this analysis to address. 144	## 6. Conclusion
145	
146	**Recommended approach:** Do not launch a permanent or full self-serve free tier now. Instead, run a time-boxed (≈30-day) full-feature trial attached to sales-qualified outbound and referral leads — reusing the existing funnel rather than building a new one — with pre-committed go/no-go conversion and cost thresholds and four named, owned tripwires (decision-date discipline, sales-cycle-length delta, cost-per-user overrun, extension-request rate) (chain C6). Use the pilot's measured results to replace this analysis's estimated and unverified cost-model inputs (chain C2) with real, sourced numbers before deciding on anything broader.
147	
148	**Key insight:** A free tier is a *conversion* mechanism, not a *demand-generation* mechanism — its revenue impact is the product of funnel volume, conversion rate, and converted LTV, and if funnel volume is zero the other two terms are irrelevant (chain C1). This company's GTM motion (outbound + referral) currently supplies that volume at or near zero for a public free tier, which is why "add a free tier" is the wrong frame; "get a company-specific conversion-rate measurement cheaply, inside the motion that already works" (chain C5/C6) is the right one.
149	
150	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** The recommended trial is not free of risk — it carries real, if bounded, sales-cycle-lengthening and cost-overrun exposure (chain C4), and it deliberately defers the two biggest upside scenarios (a real inbound/PLG motion, or full competitive parity) rather than capturing them immediately. It also does not resolve the "competitors all have one" perception question (chain C3) — a prospect who wants to self-serve evaluate today still cannot, during the trial design and rollout window.

Analyze from first principles: should our B2B SaaS product add a free tier?

Ground-truth facts (verified, not assumptions):
- Current state: $2.4M ARR from 240 paying teams, ~$10,000/team/year average contract value.
- Go-to-market: outbound sales + referrals only. No self-serve inbound channel exists today.
- Cost structure: Finance has confirmed that free-tier infrastructure and support costs scale with active users (not paying users) — i.e., a free tier is not cost-free even with zero conversions, since free users still consume infra/support.
- Unknown: we have never run a freemium pilot, so we have no empirical free-to-paid conversion rate for our product/market. Any conversion assumption is speculative, not historical.
- Competitive context: all named competitors currently offer a free tier.

Please decompose this into its foundational components and reason upward to a recommendation. In particular I want the analysis to address:
1. What problem is a free tier actually solving for — is it a distribution/acquisition mechanism, a competitive-parity/perception play, a product-led-growth motion, or something else — and does that match how this company currently acquires customers (outbound + referral, no inbound funnel to feed a free tier into)?
2. The cost side: since costs scale with active (not paying) users, model what has to be true (conversion rate, support cost per free user, infra cost per free user, funnel volume) for a free tier to be NPV-positive, given the $10K ACV anchor.
3. Second-order effects: sales motion cannibalization (does free undercut the outbound sales pitch / give prospects an excuse to stall), support team load, brand/positioning effects of "everyone else has one" (is this actually evidence it's necessary, or survivorship/mimicry?).
4. The "no pilot data" problem specifically — what's the cheapest way to get real signal before committing to a full free tier (e.g., a time-boxed trial, limited pilot, free tier for a narrow ICP segment) versus going straight to a full freemium launch.
5. A clear recommendation: add it / don't add it / conditional path — and the specific condition(s) that would flip the recommendation.

Keep the final output focused and decision-useful for a B2B SaaS founder/operator — not an exhaustive essay. Use the full first-principles method (decompose to verified truths, challenge assumptions, apply relevant companion techniques like inversion, pre-mortem, trade-off analysis, second-order thinking, estimation) but report the output concisely: ground truths, key challenged assumptions, the cost model logic, and the final recommendation with its flip condition(s).

content.text:
Stopping the file-formatting work as instructed. Here is the concise, decision-useful analysis directly.

## Ground truths (as given, with one important caveat)

- **GT-1**: $2.4M ARR, 240 paying teams, ~$10K average ACV.
- **GT-2**: 100% outbound + referral GTM; **no self-serve inbound channel exists today.**
- **GT-3**: Free-tier infra/support cost scales with *active* users, not paying users (Finance-confirmed) — a free tier is never literally free.
- **GT-4**: No historical free-to-paid conversion data exists; any conversion rate is speculative.
- **GT-5**: All named competitors have a free tier.

Caveat: these are the operator's own stipulated figures, not independently sourced by me (no CRM/Finance export opened) — treat them as solid in practice, but they are "stated," not "audited."

## Key challenged assumptions

| Assumption | Verdict |
|---|---|
| A free tier is a distribution/acquisition mechanism | **Discard** — a free tier *converts* existing top-of-funnel traffic; it doesn't generate it. With no inbound channel (GT-2), there's nothing to convert. |
| A free tier = a PLG motion that can bolt onto outbound | **Discard** — PLG needs self-serve signup infra *and* traffic feeding it; neither exists. This is a real build project, not a toggle. |
| "All competitors have one, so we need one" | **Challenge** — likely mimicry/survivorship. Competitors' free tiers are load-bearing to *different* (lower-ACV, higher-volume, self-serve) GTM motions. No win-loss data shows any deal was actually lost over this. |
| Free-tier converts will look like our $10K-ACV buyer | **Challenge** — self-selecting free signups in an outbound-qualified motion typically skew smaller/cheaper than the existing base. |
| A free tier will cannibalize outbound sales | **Challenge, plausible but unverified** — gives prospects a stalling/de-risking option; mechanism is well-known in B2B SaaS, magnitude here is unmeasured. |

## Cost-model logic (the core quantitative result)

Revenue impact of a free tier ≈ **N (signups) × r (conversion rate) × LTV (converted customer)**. If N ≈ 0 (true today, per GT-2), the other two terms don't matter — this is why "add a free tier" is the wrong frame for this company *right now*.

For the unit economics alone (ignoring N), breakeven conversion rate:
**r\* = (cost per active free user × avg. tenure as free) / LTV of a converted customer**

Using defensible brackets (cost $50–500/yr, mid $200; tenure 0.5–2.5yr, mid 1.5yr; converted LTV $9K–24K, discounted from the $10K ACV since free converts likely skew smaller, mid $15K):

- Central case: r\* ≈ **2.0%** — inside the typical 1–5% range cited for B2B self-serve freemium, so plausible but not safely so.
- Pessimistic cost case: r\* ≈ **8.3%** — above what's realistic.
- Optimistic cost case: r\* ≈ **0.3%** — trivially achievable.

**The breakeven math doesn't depend on funnel volume N at all** — only cost/user, tenure, and LTV. So volume determines how much is at stake, not whether the economics work. Since none of GT-7/8/9 (the cost, tenure, LTV inputs) have ever been measured by this company, this is the single biggest open question — bigger than the funnel problem, in terms of deciding "is this even viable."

## Second-order effects

- **Sales cannibalization**: a free/self-serve option gives active-pipeline prospects a lower-commitment alternative to a signed $10K contract; reps may lean on it as a crutch to avoid hard closes; procurement may use it to stall. Real risk, unverified magnitude.
- **Support load**: costs scale with active users (GT-3) — an unmetered, undifferentiated free cohort can blow past the cost-model's own assumptions and degrade support SLA for *paying* customers during any marketing-driven signup spike.
- **"Everyone else has one"**: weak evidence of necessity for this company specifically — it's evidence their free tier is structural to *their* (different) GTM motion, not evidence this company's outbound/referral motion needs one. No win-loss data ties any lost deal to this.

## Cheapest way to get real signal (before any full commitment)

Compared four options (full freemium launch / narrow-ICP perpetual free tier / time-boxed trial / status quo) on signal quality, build cost, cost exposure, sales-motion risk, speed, and reversibility: a **time-boxed (~30-day) full-feature trial attached to sales-qualified outbound/referral leads** dominates — it reuses the existing funnel (no new infra build), bounds cost exposure to a fixed window, and isolates the one unknown that matters (conversion rate) without also having to solve the funnel-building problem simultaneously. Going straight to full freemium conflates two different unknowns (does the product convert? does an inbound funnel even exist?) and get an ambiguous read on both for a much higher build cost and open-ended cost exposure.

Guardrails that matter if you run it: pre-commit go/no-go thresholds *before* launch (otherwise it drifts into a permanent unmanaged free tier with no decision ever made), meter/tag trial-user cost separately from day one, keep it sales-qualified rather than public self-serve, and track sales-cycle-length delta as a cannibalization tripwire.

## Recommendation and flip conditions

**Don't launch a permanent or full self-serve free tier now.** Run the time-boxed, sales-attached trial described above, with pre-committed thresholds, and use its *measured* results to replace the estimated cost-model inputs before deciding on anything broader. Confidence: **MEDIUM** — the "wrong frame" structural argument (no funnel to convert) is solid; the conditional trial recommendation is capped by the unmeasured cost/conversion brackets it's specifically designed to resolve.

- **Flips to YES** (broader/permanent free tier) if: the trial measures a sustained conversion rate ≥ the measured breakeven r\*, across ≥2 cohorts, **and** no material sales-cycle lengthening/ACV erosion shows up, **and** a real inbound-traffic source exists or is being built (volume still has to come from somewhere).
- **Flips to an outright NO** (skip even the trial) if: Finance's *measured* cost-per-active-free-user implies a breakeven r\* above ~8–10% — at that point the economics fail regardless of execution quality.

- **GT-2**: 100% outbound + referral GTM; **no self-serve inbound channel exists today.**
- **GT-3**: Free-tier infra/support cost scales with *active* users, not paying users (Finance-confirmed) — a free tier is never literally free.
- **GT-4**: No historical free-to-paid conversion data exists; any conversion rate is speculative.
- **GT-5**: All named competitors have a free tier.

Caveat: these are the operator's own stipulated figures, not independently sourced by me (no CRM/Finance export opened) — treat them as solid in practice, but they are "stated," not "audited."

## Key challenged assumptions

| Assumption | Verdict |
|---|---|
| A free tier is a distribution/acquisition mechanism | **Discard** — a free tier *converts* existing top-of-funnel traffic; it doesn't generate it. With no inbound channel (GT-2), there's nothing to convert. |
| A free tier = a PLG motion that can bolt onto outbound | **Discard** — PLG needs self-serve signup infra *and* traffic feeding it; neither exists. This is a real build project, not a toggle. |
| "All competitors have one, so we need one" | **Challenge** — likely mimicry/survivorship. Competitors' free tiers are load-bearing to *different* (lower-ACV, higher-volume, self-serve) GTM motions. No win-loss data shows any deal was actually lost over this. |
| Free-tier converts will look like our $10K-ACV buyer | **Challenge** — self-selecting free signups in an outbound-qualified motion typically skew smaller/cheaper than the existing base. |
| A free tier will cannibalize outbound sales | **Challenge, plausible but unverified** — gives prospects a stalling/de-risking option; mechanism is well-known in B2B SaaS, magnitude here is unmeasured. |

## Cost-model logic (the core quantitative result)

Revenue impact of a free tier ≈ **N (signups) × r (conversion rate) × LTV (converted customer)**. If N ≈ 0 (true today, per GT-2), the other two terms don't matter — this is why "add a free tier" is the wrong frame for this company *right now*.

For the unit economics alone (ignoring N), breakeven conversion rate:
**r\* = (cost per active free user × avg. tenure as free) / LTV of a converted customer**

Using defensible brackets (cost $50–500/yr, mid $200; tenure 0.5–2.5yr, mid 1.5yr; converted LTV $9K–24K, discounted from the $10K ACV since free converts likely skew smaller, mid $15K):

- Central case: r\* ≈ **2.0%** — inside the typical 1–5% range cited for B2B self-serve freemium, so plausible but not safely so.
- Pessimistic cost case: r\* ≈ **8.3%** — above what's realistic.
- Optimistic cost case: r\* ≈ **0.3%** — trivially achievable.

**The breakeven math doesn't depend on funnel volume N at all** — only cost/user, tenure, and LTV. So volume determines how much is at stake, not whether the economics work. Since none of GT-7/8/9 (the cost, tenure, LTV inputs) have ever been measured by this company, this is the single biggest open question — bigger than the funnel problem, in terms of deciding "is this even viable."

## Second-order effects

- **Sales cannibalization**: a free/self-serve option gives active-pipeline prospects a lower-commitment alternative to a signed $10K contract; reps may lean on it as a crutch to avoid hard closes; procurement may use it to stall. Real risk, unverified magnitude.
- **Support load**: costs scale with active users (GT-3) — an unmetered, undifferentiated free cohort can blow past the cost-model's own assumptions and degrade support SLA for *paying* customers during any marketing-driven signup spike.
- **"Everyone else has one"**: weak evidence of necessity for this company specifically — it's evidence their free tier is structural to *their* (different) GTM motion, not evidence this company's outbound/referral motion needs one. No win-loss data ties any lost deal to this.

## Cheapest way to get real signal (before any full commitment)

Compared four options (full freemium launch / narrow-ICP perpetual free tier / time-boxed trial / status quo) on signal quality, build cost, cost exposure, sales-motion risk, speed, and reversibility: a **time-boxed (~30-day) full-feature trial attached to sales-qualified outbound/referral leads** dominates — it reuses the existing funnel (no new infra build), bounds cost exposure to a fixed window, and isolates the one unknown that matters (conversion rate) without also having to solve the funnel-building problem simultaneously. Going straight to full freemium conflates two different unknowns (does the product convert? does an inbound funnel even exist?) and get an ambiguous read on both for a much higher build cost and open-ended cost exposure.

Guardrails that matter if you run it: pre-commit go/no-go thresholds *before* launch (otherwise it drifts into a permanent unmanaged free tier with no decision ever made), meter/tag trial-user cost separately from day one, keep it sales-qualified rather than public self-serve, and track sales-cycle-length delta as a cannibalization tripwire.

## Recommendation and flip conditions

**Don't launch a permanent or full self-serve free tier now.** Run the time-boxed, sales-attached trial described above, with pre-committed thresholds, and use its *measured* results to replace the estimated cost-model inputs before deciding on anything broader. Confidence: **MEDIUM** — the "wrong frame" structural argument (no funnel to convert) is solid; the conditional trial recommendation is capped by the unmeasured cost/conversion brackets it's specifically designed to resolve.

- **Flips to YES** (broader/permanent free tier) if: the trial measures a sustained conversion rate ≥ the measured breakeven r\*, across ≥2 cohorts, **and** no material sales-cycle lengthening/ACV erosion shows up, **and** a real inbound-traffic source exists or is being built (volume still has to come from somewhere).
- **Flips to an outright NO** (skip even the trial) if: Finance's *measured* cost-per-active-free-user implies a breakeven r\* above ~8–10% — at that point the economics fail regardless of execution quality.
